# Literature Overview

Noise pollution is a omnipresent environmental externality, yet its consequences for human capital formation remain largely unexplored relative to other pollutants. We situate our contribution within three literatures: causal evidence on other environmental pollutants and human capital, the economics of noise as an externality affecting well-being, productivity, and health, and the small existing body of work on noise and human capital specifically, whose identification challenges we aim to address.

## Other Environmental Pollutants and Human Capital
A parallel economics literature documents comparable causal effects of other pollutants — chiefly particulate matter and extreme heat — on human capital formation. A recent meta-analysis pools the causal evidence across 28 studies and finds an average penalty of -0.022 SD [@nguyenEffectAirPollution2026]. Effects operate across the life course: early-life particulate exposure lowers long-run schooling [@sandersWhatDoesntKill2012] and earnings [@isenEveryBreathYou2017], while temporary exposure during schooling or high-stakes exams lowers test scores, with downstream effects on educational attainment and wages [@ebensteinLongRunEconomicConsequences2016]. Similar effects are documented for extreme heat [@parkLearningInhibitedHeat2020]. For the pollution channel, a smaller but growing literature shows the damage is at least partly abatable through filtration [@gilraineAirFiltersPollution2025; @bonanEffectAirPurifiers2024]. This literature establishes that environmental disturbances can leave lasting marks on human capital. The question we ask is whether the same holds for noise.

## Noise, Wellbeing, and Productivity
The literature on the effects of noise pollution is considerably smaller. Economic scholars have studied it as an environmental externality affecting well-being, productivity, and asset prices. @vanpraagUsingHappinessSurveys2005 use happiness surveys to value aircraft noise around Amsterdam Airport, showing that noise reduces subjective well-being and that these welfare losses are not necessarily fully capitalized into house prices. @deanNoiseCognitiveFunction2024 provides experimental evidence from textile workers in Kenya that a 7 dB increase in workplace noise reduces output by about 3 percent, impairs cognitive function, and that workers do not fully recognize the productivity cost of noisy working conditions. @henerNoisePollutionViolent2022 exploits daily variation in aircraft landing approaches at Frankfurt Airport and finds that higher aircraft noise increases violent crime, particularly physical assaults. @krekelDoesPresenceWind2017 combine SOEP household panel data with wind turbine locations in Germany and find that nearby turbine construction reduces residential life satisfaction — with effects concentrated within about 4 km and fading after at most five years. Two studies isolate the effect of noise on property values specifically, with consistent implications in opposite directions: @allroggenPlanesOverheadHow2025 show that technical flight path adaptation at three US airports decreased property values where it increased noise, while @morettiTrafficNoiseExternality2025 find that the construction of highway noise barriers in Florida — which reduce noise — increased affected property values.

## Noise, Health, and Sleep
Research in public health and epidemiology has found impacts on metabolic, cardiovascular, and mental health [@welchHealthEffectsTransport2023]. Most relevant to our research is the evidence on sleep: a systematic review of environmental noise and sleep finds transportation noise disturbs objectively measured sleep, and disturbs self-reported sleep specifically when survey questions reference noise explicitly [@basnerWHOEnvironmentalNoise2018]. In a direct demonstration of the objective effect, @basnerNocturnalAircraftNoise2008 uses a laboratory design and shows that nocturnal aircraft noise significantly increases objectively measured next-morning sleepiness. @griefahnNoiseEmittedRoad2006 compare road, rail, and aircraft noise in a sleep-laboratory setting and find that transport noise worsens subjective sleep quality and reaction time, while physiological sleep disruption differs by noise source. @bodinAnnoyanceSleepConcentration2015 study combined road and railway traffic noise in Malmö and find that access to a quiet side of the dwelling is associated with lower noise annoyance, fewer concentration problems, and better sleep when the bedroom faces the quiet side. @trimmelEffectsLowIntensity2012 experimentally expose participants to low-intensity aircraft or neighbourhood noise and find impaired text learning together with physiological stress responses, especially under aircraft noise.

A set of studies exploits quasi-random variation to strengthen causal claims on health [@nybergAirNoisePollution2025]. @boesAIRCRAFTNOISEHEALTH2013 exploit unexpected changes in flight regulations at Zurich airport and find that higher aircraft noise increases self-reported sleeping problems and headaches. @beghelliHealthBenefitsReducing2023 use unannounced changes in early-morning aircraft landings at Heathrow and find reductions in medication expenditures for central nervous system and respiratory conditions when noise exposure falls. @argysResidentialNoiseExposure2020 utilize exogenous variation in a US flight path policy concentrating air traffic to show that the resulting noise increased low birth weight occurrences. @wangImpactAeroplaneNoise2022 study aircraft noise in New York and find increases in insomnia, adult cardiovascular disease, and depression, as well as mental-health- and substance-use-related healthcare utilization. @krekelWindTurbinesHave2023 find no corresponding evidence that turbines worsen general, mental, or physical health, doctor visits, or sleep. @greenhillNoisePollutionInfant2026 utilizes changes in wind direction redirecting train noise exposure in California to identify strong impacts on infant health. @lindgrenSoundEnvironmentHealth2021 evaluates a Swedish road traffic noise mitigation program and finds delayed but substantial reductions in cardiovascular diagnoses, primarily driven by hypertension. @zouWindTurbineSyndrome2020 studies US wind farm installations and finds increases in suicide rates, with evidence suggesting sleep disruption from low-frequency noise as a possible mechanism.

## Noise and Human Capital
There also exists a small body of work on the impacts of noise on human capital formation. A key challenge in identifying such effects is causality. In particular, we expect noise pollution to be priced in the rental market, causing residential sorting. In equilibrium, individuals with higher tolerance or lower income will be exposed to noise at a higher rate. If this is not accounted for, estimates of the impact of noise pollution will not be representative of the impact on the average citizen or be confounded with other relevant behavior. Avoidance behavior might also be problematic if it is heterogeneous across third factors with a direct link to health. Additionally, exposure to noise might be correlated with air pollution and (extreme) weather, causing further confounding. The existing body of research outlined below does not fully address these challenges.
@hainesChronicAircraftNoise2001 study schoolchildren near London Heathrow and find that chronic aircraft noise exposure is associated with higher annoyance and poorer reading comprehension, but not with worse mental health or elevated cortisol. @hyggeProspectiveStudyEffects2002 exploit the opening and closure of Munich airports and find that aircraft noise impairs children's reading and long-term memory, while cognitive performance improves after noise exposure ceases. @clarkEffectsRoadTraffic2010 use the cross-country RANCH data and find that aircraft noise is linearly associated with worse recognition memory in children, while road traffic noise shows different and more mixed associations with episodic memory. @klatteEffectsAircraftNoise2017 study primary school children around Frankfurt Airport and find that even comparatively moderate aircraft noise exposure is associated with lower reading performance, higher annoyance, and worse quality of life.

None of these four studies resolves all challenges simultaneously. @hainesChronicAircraftNoise2001 match high- and low-noise schools on age, existing school-level sound insulation, deprivation, and ethnicity, but the matching operates at the school level — it does not address self-selection of families into noisy versus quiet homes within catchment areas — and the study includes no measure of avoidance behavior (e.g., insulation or quiet-facing bedrooms) or of co-varying air pollution and weather. @hyggeProspectiveStudyEffects2002 come closest to addressing sorting: because the source of noise variation is the relocation of Munich's airport rather than families relocating, exposure changes independently of residential choice. But the design still cannot separate noise from co-occurring changes in aircraft-related air pollution at the same sites, includes no avoidance-behavior measure, and — as @klatteEffectsAircraftNoise2017 note in their own critique of this study — relies on small, unevenly attriting subsamples and an undocumented exclusion of poor readers from the reading-score analysis. @clarkEffectsRoadTraffic2010 improve on individual-level confounding by adjusting for mother's education, employment, crowding, and home ownership, and are unusual in directly controlling for classroom window glazing as a proxy for sound insulation — but the design is cross-sectional, so sorting into noise-exposed catchment areas on unobserved family traits is not resolved by covariate adjustment, and air pollution and weather remain uncontrolled; @klatteEffectsAircraftNoise2017 further note that they do not account for clustering of children within schools and classes, risking overstated significance. @klatteEffectsAircraftNoise2017 address that clustering problem with multilevel models and combine individual- and class-level socioeconomic controls more completely than prior work, and separately control for acute noise at the time of testing to avoid conflating chronic and acute exposure — but their design is likewise cross-sectional across noise-exposed areas, so residential sorting is addressed only insofar as it correlates with the included socioeconomic covariates, and neither avoidance behavior nor air pollution and weather are measured. We address these remaining sorting, avoidance-behavior, and confounding concerns by exploiting the staggered, plausibly exogenous timing of the BoViT insulation and noise-barrier rollout described below.

# Data

## Exposure
We identify exposure to noise pollution using the staggered rollout of mitigation technology. The Swedish transportation authority (Trafikverket) provides dwellings and neighborhoods with sound insulation and noise barriers, respectively. Obtaining data on the provision of these measures is a prerequisite for our analysis.
The BoViT noise mitigation program includes information on all provided insulation and barriers, most notably identifying the exact dwellings that received insulation, as well as the date of provision. This data is not publicly available and will have to be requested from Trafikverket.
A smaller subset covering only noise barriers is publicly available. Inspection of this data revealed that construction dates are missing for a large share of barriers; these gaps could potentially be closed with Trafikverket's assistance, but the BoViT data should be prioritized where possible.
Supplementary data on dwelling, road, and rail positions is publicly available. We can also request cross-sectional modeled noise exposure for the entire country, as well as historical traffic density data at measurement points. This will allow us to control for background noise exposure and traffic density in our analysis.
